overview.title: Student & Teacher Overview: Lesson 22
overview.text: In this lesson, you will solve systems of two linear equations in two variables. A solution to a system is an ordered pair $(x, y)$ that satisfies both equations simultaneously. Graphically, this corresponds to the unique point of intersection between two lines.
outcomes: Identify solutions to simultaneous linear equations graphically as intersection points.
Solve systems of linear equations algebraically using the substitution method.
Classify systems as consistent-independent (one solution), inconsistent (parallel, no solution), or consistent-dependent (coincident, infinitely many solutions).
overview.teacherInsight: Connect systems of equations to compound sentences: a system of two equations is simply Equation 1 AND Equation 2. Both conditions must hold.

content.html:
Three Geometric Possibilities for 2×2 Linear Systems

1. Unique Solution

Lines have different slopes and intersect at exactly one point $(x, y)$.

2. No Solution (Inconsistent)

Lines have identical slopes but different y-intercepts (parallel lines). No intersection.

3. Infinitely Many Solutions

Equations are equivalent multiples. Lines are coincident (share every point).

vocabulary.definition: A collection of two or more linear equations involving the same set of variables.
A single point on the coordinate plane where two lines cross, representing the simultaneous solution.
An algebraic technique where one variable is isolated and substituted into the other equation.

practiceQuestions.question: Solve the system using substitution: $y = 2x - 1$ and $3x + y = 9$.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Substitute $2x - 1$ for $y$ in second equation: $3x + (2x - 1) = 9 \implies 5x - 1 = 9 \implies 5x = 10 \implies x = 2$. Then $y = 2(2) - 1 = 3$. The solution is $(2, 3)$.

practiceQuestions.question: What is the graphical relationship between $2x + y = 4$ and $4x + 2y = 12$?
options: They are parallel lines with no solution.
They intersect at a single point $(2, 0)$.
They are identical coincident lines with infinite solutions.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Rewrite in slope-intercept form: $y = -2x + 4$ and $y = -2x + 6$. Both have slope $m = -2$ but different y-intercepts (4 vs 6), so they are parallel lines with no intersection.
